grounded_facts: Elizabeth shifts from authority to supplication, framing his departure as a personal abandonment during a time of looming crisis.
Elizabeth appeals to Raleigh as a friend, asking him not to abandon her as 'storm clouds' gather.
memories.memory_text: I shifted from commanding him to pleading, asking Raleigh not to abandon me as a friend when the storm clouds are gathering—I could see he was looking away, and I felt so old and unseen.

grounded_facts: Queen Elizabeth arrives by barge to consult Dr Dee on astrological matters, continuing a prior pattern of seeking his counsel.
memories.memory_text: I arrived by barge to consult Dr Dee on astrological matters, continuing my practice of seeking his counsel.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth speaks from the barge, announcing her return to seek Dr Dee's astrological counsel.
memories.memory_text: I spoke from the barge, announcing my return to seek Dr Dee's astrological counsel.

grounded_facts: Dr Dee distinguishes between Elizabeth's mortality as a person and the eternal nature of her queenship, offering mystical validation of her rule.
memories.memory_text: I heard Dr Dee say that Elizabeth is mortal, but the Queen will never die, and I understood then that my life as a woman is fleeting, while the crown I bear transcends death.

grounded_facts: Dr Dee interprets unusual planetary alignments as signifying the rise and fall of empires, though he cannot specify which ones, framing it as an astrological omen with political and personal implications for Elizabeth.
memories.memory_text: I listened as Dr Dee spoke of unusual planetary alignments, saying they foretold the rise of a great empire and the fall of another, though he could not say which — I felt deep within me that my moment of destiny is near.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth asserts authority by ordering Walsingham to leave, creating space for a private conversation with Dr Dee.
memories.memory_text: I asserted my authority by telling Francis to leave us, so I could speak privately with Dr Dee.

grounded_facts: Dr Dee shifts from celestial charts to reading Elizabeth's facial features as a symbolic chart, revealing inner strength, love, and emerging fear, marking a transition from public prophecy to private spiritual insight.
memories.memory_text: I saw Dr Dee shift from studying the celestial charts to quietly observing my face as if it were a map of my soul, murmuring about my character and revealing inner strength and love, marking a moment when our exchange turned from public prophecy to private insight.

grounded_facts: Dr Dee directly names Elizabeth's inner fear and self-doubt, disrupting her composure and marking a shift in their interaction from formal to intimate.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Dr Dee that I doubt myself and that he had not seen fear in my face before, which unsettled me and made me ask if I had reason to fear, marking the moment our interaction became intimate and disrupted my composure.

grounded_facts: A private session between Dr Dee and Queen Elizabeth following a public astrological discussion, during which Dee offers personal readings and spiritual counsel.
memories.memory_text: After I told Francis to leave, I asked Dr Dee privately about what the stars foretold for me as a woman and a queen, and though he said he saw only shadows and that astrology is an art, not a science, I understood.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth is returning down the Thames on a royal barge at dusk, sitting in silence and absorbed in thought.
memories.memory_text: I returned down the Thames on my barge at dusk, sitting in silence and lost in my thoughts.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth removes her shift and stands naked before the mirror.
memories.memory_text: I removed my shift and stood naked before the mirror, alone in my dressing chamber by lamplight.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth looks at her naked reflection in the mirror.
memories.memory_text: I looked at my naked reflection in the mirror and saw myself as I am.

grounded_facts: Raleigh implies criticism of Elizabeth's demand for obedience, questioning whether she thinks it wrong that her ladies jump at her command.
memories.memory_text: I heard Raleigh question whether I expect my ladies to jump at my command, as if obedience were something to be criticized.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth admits to Raleigh that she is sometimes tired of being in control, revealing a moment of vulnerability.
memories.memory_text: I admitted to Mr. Raleigh that there are times when I'm tired of being always in control, and I let myself speak the truth I so often keep hidden.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth commands Raleigh to dance with Bess, asserting her authority and setting up a moment of controlled intimacy.
memories.memory_text: I commanded Bess to dance with Mr. Raleigh, making it clear that he was eager to show his skill, and I felt the weight of my own authority in orchestrating the moment.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth personally demonstrates and explains the steps of La Volta to Raleigh, emphasizing physical contact and timing.
memories.memory_text: I showed Raleigh how to perform La Volta, instructing him on where to place his hands and how to swing his partner on the eighth step, making the dance seem simple under my guidance.

grounded_facts: A dance lesson and performance of La Volta in the Queen's private quarters, involving courtiers, musicians, and royal participation.
Bess is instructed in and performs the La Volta dance under the Queen's supervision, demonstrating fearlessness and enjoyment.
memories.memory_text: I watched Bess learn and perform the La Volta in my private quarters, where the dancing master spun her boldly and Raleigh joined to swing her round with growing ease, all under my observation as queen.

grounded_facts: Walsingham enters and is quietly ordered by Elizabeth to leave Bess and Raleigh undisturbed, showing her control over surveillance and intervention.
memories.memory_text: I saw Walsingham enter and position himself nearby, watching closely, so I quietly told him to leave Bess and Raleigh alone—I made it clear they were not to be disturbed.

grounded_facts: A formal royal movement from the Presence Chamber to the Chapel Royal, part of the Queen’s daily religious observance, attended by courtiers and guarded by bodyguards.
memories.memory_text: I was processing from the Presence Chamber to the Chapel Royal, surrounded by courtiers and guarded by my bodyguards, as part of my daily observance.

grounded_facts: Ramsay shouts a treasonous slogan declaring Mary the true queen, directly opposing Elizabeth’s legitimacy in her presence.
Ramsay shouts a proclamation supporting Mary as England's true queen, directly challenging Elizabeth's authority in a public and sacred setting.
memories.memory_text: I heard Ramsay shout 'God for Mary! England's true Queen!' in my presence, a direct and treasonous challenge to my authority during the procession.

grounded_facts: A group of ladies are kneeling in the chapel, suggesting a religious or ceremonial gathering interrupted by Babington's intrusion.
memories.memory_text: I saw a line of my ladies kneeling in the chapel just before the intrusion.

grounded_facts: Babington enters the chapel and points a pistol at Elizabeth, initiating a life-threatening confrontation.
memories.memory_text: I turned and faced Babington as he pointed a pistol at me, calling out my name with a look of fixation.

grounded_facts: Babington shoots at Elizabeth in the chapel, but the shot misses or fails to injure her; he collapses in anguish afterward.
memories.memory_text: I heard the shot and felt no injury—I remained standing while Babington cried out and collapsed to the ground.

grounded_facts: A private moment between Queen Elizabeth and Bess in the queen's chambers, marked by introspection and emotional tension regarding Mary's fate.
memories.memory_text: I sat deep in thought in my chambers with Bess by my side, shadows all around, and I could feel the weight of the decision ahead, though I dismissed any thought of my own appearance with a shrug.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth expresses doubt and frustration over Mary's continued denial of guilt, questioning why she won't admit wrongdoing despite evidence.
memories.memory_text: I told Bess that I can be merciful, but I am troubled because Mary protests her innocence, and I believe that is a lie—yet I cannot understand why she will not admit she has wronged me.

grounded_facts: Bess insists that Mary will continue lying until executed, showing a shift toward ruthlessness.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed Bess insist that Mary will keep lying until I have her executed, and I stared at her in surprise, seeing how hardened she has become.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth remarks that Bess used to be gentler, noting her increased severity.
memories.memory_text: I remarked to Bess that she used to be gentler, because I've noticed how much more severe she has become.

grounded_facts: A formal commission of lords convenes to try Mary Stuart in the Great Hall of Fotheringay Castle.
memories.memory_text: I inferred that a formal commission of lords had convened to try me in the Great Hall of Fotheringay Castle, judging by the sombre setting and the group of lords facing me.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth refuses to accept the necessity of Mary Stuart's execution and challenges the authority behind the order.
memories.memory_text: I refused to accept that Mary Stuart must die, questioning aloud who dares command me as Queen.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth rebukes Walsingham for overstepping, questioning who dares command her, and tells him to go home.
memories.memory_text: I rebuked Walsingham for overstepping, telling him no one gives orders to me and that he should go home to his wife and bed.

grounded_facts: Walsingham insists that the law must be followed, implying Mary Stuart's execution is legally mandated.
memories.memory_text: I was told the law must have its way, implying that Mary Stuart's execution is legally required.

grounded_facts: Recognizing futility, Walsingham ends the argument and leaves the chamber.
memories.memory_text: I saw Walsingham recognize the futility of arguing further, bow, and leave the chamber.

grounded_facts: A private meeting between Queen Elizabeth and Sir Walter Raleigh in her chambers, where deep personal and political matters are discussed.
memories.memory_text: I was sitting alone in my chambers, lost in thought, when I sensed Raleigh enter; I didn't turn to face him, but I knew it was him, and I kept my back to him as we began to speak.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth suspects Raleigh has come to pressure her to execute Mary, like others have.
memories.memory_text: I suspected Raleigh had come like others, pressing me to order Mary's death, and I asked him directly if Bess had sent him to tell me I must murder a queen.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth admits her fear and internal struggle over executing another queen, revealing her emotional and spiritual burden.
memories.memory_text: I admitted to Raleigh that I am afraid — I said it aloud, that I am always afraid, carrying this fear of what it means to execute another queen and the weight it places on my soul.

grounded_facts: Raleigh comforts Elizabeth by asserting that queens are mortal, reducing the spiritual weight of executing Mary.
Raleigh articulates that queens, though near divine, are mortal, implying that executing Mary is a human, not sacrilegious, act.
memories.memory_text: I remember Raleigh speaking to me, saying I didn't need instruction in my duty, and then telling me that though royalty is close to immortality, queens are mortal—his way of comforting me, I suppose, by making the act of executing Mary feel less like a sin against the divine and more like a human necessity.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth recognizes that Raleigh deeply understands her inner conflict.
memories.memory_text: I told Raleigh that he understands me well, because I saw in him a rare awareness of the conflict within me.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth acknowledges her obligation to England and implicitly accepts the necessity of executing Mary, though at spiritual cost.
memories.memory_text: I said I owe England my life, but I refused to give more—I made it clear I won't surrender my soul.

grounded_facts: A formal execution event held in the great hall of Fotheringay Castle, attended by dignitaries, members of Parliament, and the public.
memories.memory_text: I inferred that a formal execution event was being held in the great hall of Fotheringay Castle, attended by dignitaries, members of Parliament, and the public, based on the arrangements I heard about.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth is unable to rest or find peace, pacing in increasing agitation after realizing what is happening.
memories.memory_text: I know what is happening, and I can't rest or find peace — I tried to sit, but I keep pacing, feeling more agitated with every step.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth, visibly distressed, emerges from the Privy Chamber and urgently demands that something be stopped upon seeing Raleigh.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Elizabeth, visibly distressed, emerges from the Privy Chamber and urgently demands that something be stopped upon seeing Raleigh.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth, in emotional distress, directly speaks to Raleigh, demanding that something be stopped.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Elizabeth, in emotional distress, directly speaks to Raleigh, demanding that something be stopped.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth shouts in hysteria, demanding that something be stopped, while being physically restrained by Raleigh.
Elizabeth becomes hysterical and shouts desperately, indicating emotional distress and urgency about an ongoing situation.
memories.memory_text: I was hysterical, shouting desperately while Raleigh held me back, because I needed to stop what was about to happen.

grounded_facts: Raleigh and Bess physically support Elizabeth as she collapses in grief, forming a unifying embrace.
memories.memory_text: I felt Raleigh and Bess catch me as I fell, their arms holding me up, and for a moment, I let myself be held in that shared embrace.

grounded_facts: A moment of collective emotional response following the off-screen execution, marked by Elizabeth's breakdown and shared embrace with Raleigh and Bess.
Elizabeth reacts with intense grief as if physically struck by the execution axe, collapsing into the arms of Raleigh and Bess.
memories.memory_text: I cried out as if the axe had struck my own neck, and in that moment, I collapsed into sobs, overwhelmed by grief I could no longer hold back.

grounded_facts: Philip delivers a passionate condemnation of Elizabeth, labeling her a 'blood-soaked virgin' and declaring she will lose her country, throne, and life.
Philip publicly declares a holy war against England in response to the martyrdom of a Christian lady, citing just and divine cause.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Philip declared a holy war against England, condemning me as a 'blood-soaked virgin' and vowing I would lose my country, throne, and life in retribution for the martyrdom of a Christian lady.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth demands to know how Walsingham has failed her, initiating the confrontation that leads to his confession.
memories.memory_text: I demanded that Walsingham tell me how he had failed me and what I was to forgive him for.

grounded_facts: Walsingham admits that his intelligence operation allowed Philip of Spain to justify war by orchestrating Mary Stuart's complicity in a murder plot.
memories.memory_text: I learned that Walsingham admitted his intelligence operation allowed Philip of Spain to justify war by letting Mary Stuart's complicity be revealed.

grounded_facts: Walsingham reveals that Philip of Spain orchestrated events so that Mary Stuart would appear guilty, providing just cause for war.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Philip of Spain orchestrated events so that Mary Stuart would be drawn into a murder plot, giving him just cause for war.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth understands that she was manipulated into ordering Mary Stuart's execution, which provides Philip of Spain with just cause for holy war.
memories.memory_text: I realized I had been manipulated into ordering Mary Stuart's execution, which made me appear as a murderer of God's anointed and gave Spain holy cause to punish me.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth tells Walsingham to go, effectively ending their interaction and his role in the moment of crisis.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Elizabeth tells Walsingham to go, effectively ending their interaction and his role in the moment of crisis.

grounded_facts: A private meeting between Elizabeth and Walsingham in which the consequences of past political actions are revealed and acknowledged.
memories.memory_text: I remember the private meeting with Walsingham, where I confronted him, heard the truth, and understood the consequences of what we had done.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth releases Walsingham from her presence, signaling the end of his influence and her emotional withdrawal.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Elizabeth releases Walsingham from her presence, signaling the end of his influence and her emotional withdrawal.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth summons Raleigh to her private quarters late at night, indicating urgency and emotional vulnerability.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Elizabeth summons Raleigh to her private quarters late at night, indicating urgency and emotional vulnerability.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth voices deep doubts about life, death, and divine justice, testing Raleigh's worldview.
memories.memory_text: I voiced my doubts about death and whether any of it means anything, watching Raleigh closely to see how he would answer.

grounded_facts: Raleigh declares his love for Elizabeth in the present world, affirming emotional truth despite impossibility.
memories.memory_text: I heard Raleigh tell me that in this world, he has loved me, and his words touched something deep within me.

grounded_facts: A private, emotionally intense encounter between Queen Elizabeth and Sir Walter Raleigh in her quarters at night, outside formal court protocol.
memories.memory_text: I remember that A private, emotionally intense encounter between Queen Elizabeth and Sir Walter Raleigh in her quarters at night, outside formal court protocol.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth indirectly asks for a kiss, framing it as a momentary, unacknowledged act outside duty and decorum.
memories.memory_text: I asked him if he would give me a kiss—something I’ve not known in a long time, something to be forgotten afterwards, just for now, outside duty and decorum.

grounded_facts: After a charged emotional exchange, Elizabeth requests and receives a kiss from Raleigh, symbolizing unfulfilled longing and mutual affection.
memories.memory_text: I asked Raleigh for a kiss, and he took me in his arms; we shared one fleeting moment that held all we could never have, and when it ended, I turned away, holding on to the memory with my eyes closed.

grounded_facts: The court at Whitehall Palace is in a state of emergency due to an invasion threat, with armed men moving quickly and valuables being removed.
memories.memory_text: I inferred that the court was in turmoil at Whitehall Palace, with armed men rushing about and valuables being moved, likely due to an invasion threat.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth cries out for air, prompting her servants to respond.
Elizabeth suddenly awakens from sleep, expressing a desperate need for air.
memories.memory_text: I suddenly woke in fear and cried out for air, needing to breathe immediately.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth moves to the open window and breathes deeply, seeking relief.
memories.memory_text: I moved to the open window and breathed in deeply, seeking relief.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth informs the council, notably surprising Walsingham, that the Spanish lack sufficient barges at Calais, buying England time.
memories.memory_text: I informed the council, notably surprising Walsingham, that the Spanish lack sufficient barges at Calais, which buys England valuable time.

grounded_facts: A high-level military meeting in the Map Room at Whitehall Palace where Elizabeth and her advisors assess the threat of the Spanish Armada and plan England's defense.
memories.memory_text: I presided over a high-level military meeting in the Map Room at Whitehall Palace, where my advisors and I assessed the threat of the Spanish Armada and began planning England's defense.

grounded_facts: Walsingham articulates the invasion plan: the Spanish fleet will escort barges carrying Parma's army across the Channel and up the Thames, warning that combined forces would overwhelm English defenses.
memories.memory_text: I was told that the Spanish fleet plans to escort barges carrying Parma's army across the Channel and up the Thames, and that if they reach Calais in strength, the combined forces would be beyond our power to resist.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth demonstrates command by analyzing the Spanish Armada's status and identifying a critical delay in their barge availability at Calais, asserting that this grants England time.
memories.memory_text: I demonstrated command by analyzing the Spanish Armada's status and identifying the critical delay in barge availability at Calais, asserting that this grants us time and that their fleet must not reach Calais.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth concludes that the Spanish fleet must be prevented from reaching Calais, establishing a clear military objective.
memories.memory_text: I concluded that the Spanish fleet must not reach Calais, and I made that my clear military objective.

grounded_facts: Howard cautions Elizabeth that the Spanish Armada is likely to break through English naval defenses and urges preparation for the worst-case scenario.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Lord Howard that the Spanish Armada would likely break through our naval defenses, and he urged me to prepare for the worst.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth counters Walsingham's question with a metaphorical assertion of her reliance on multiple intelligence sources.
Elizabeth emphasizes that she relies on more than one source of information, implying the existence of independent intelligence networks beyond Walsingham.
memories.memory_text: When Walsingham asked how I knew about the Dutch barges, I told him that I do not see with only one eye or walk on only one leg, making it clear that I rely on more than just his intelligence.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth returns from public areas of Whitehall Palace to her private chambers, accompanied by Walsingham and her entourage, followed by an interaction with her ladies-in-waiting.
memories.memory_text: I walked back from the public rooms to my private chambers with Walsingham at my side and my entourage following, and when I entered, my ladies-in-waiting rose quickly, waiting for my command.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth returns to her quarters and immediately notices that Bess is missing, indicating her attentiveness to her court's composition.
memories.memory_text: I returned to my quarters and immediately noticed Bess was missing when I scanned my ladies.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth observes Margaret and realizes she knows something about Bess's absence, indicating Elizabeth's perceptiveness.
memories.memory_text: I saw that Margaret knew something about Bess's absence the moment my eyes landed on her.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth directly asks Margaret about Bess's whereabouts after noticing her suspicious awareness.
memories.memory_text: I asked Margaret directly where Bess was after realizing she was aware of her absence.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth confronts Bess and learns that she is married and pregnant, triggering a violent outburst.
memories.memory_text: I demanded Bess answer me—was she married, was she with child?—and when she whispered 'Yes, my lady,' I was undone.

grounded_facts: In a fit of rage, Elizabeth violently strikes Bess, who endures the attack in silence.
memories.memory_text: I stormed into the room, consumed by rage, and struck Bess repeatedly, beating her about the head while she stood silent and bowed before me.

grounded_facts: A tense and violent confrontation initiated by Queen Elizabeth upon discovering Bess Throckmorton's secret marriage and pregnancy.
memories.memory_text: I stormed into the room, called out to Bess, and when I learned the truth, my rage consumed me—I could not hold back.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth declares her absolute control over Bess, comparing her to a collared dog and demanding obedience in marriage and reproduction.
memories.memory_text: I told her she has no will of her own—that my bitches wear my collars, and she must ask my permission before she marries or breeds.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth verbally attacks Bess, accusing her of treachery for marrying and becoming pregnant without royal permission.
memories.memory_text: I called her a traitress, screamed that she dares keep secrets from me, that I am her Queen, and I demanded to know—over and over—if the child was his.

grounded_facts: Raleigh quietly tells Elizabeth that her behavior does not reflect the queen he loves and serves, confronting her with moral disappointment.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Raleigh that this was not the queen he loves and serves, and his quiet words struck me deeply.

grounded_facts: Raleigh silently witnesses the scene and then speaks, expressing sorrow and disapproval of Elizabeth's conduct, which leads to her regaining composure.
memories.memory_text: I saw Raleigh watching me with sorrow and disapproval, and in his unflinching gaze, I felt my madness fade and found myself again.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth formally accuses Raleigh of seducing a lady under her care and orders his arrest.
memories.memory_text: I confronted Raleigh and demanded the truth about his marriage and whether Bess was with child; I declared he had seduced a lady under my care and married without my consent, so I ordered Walsingham to arrest him.

grounded_facts: A private meeting between Elizabeth and Dr Dee in which she seeks clarity and hope from his prophetic knowledge amid rising tension.
Elizabeth confronts Dr Dee about the meaning of his prophecy, rejecting the idea that the English empire will fall under her reign and demanding a reinterpretation.
Elizabeth aggressively questions Dr Dee's prophecy, accusing him of delivering undesirable fate rather than empowering truth.
memories.memory_text: I confronted Dr Dee in his chambers, demanding he reinterpret his prophecy—I would not let England fall under my reign, nor be a toy of the fates, and when I saw his quizzical gaze, I let my rage pass and asked only for hope, for certainty must not bind me.

grounded_facts: Dr Dee responds to Elizabeth's demand for hope by describing how individuals respond differently in crisis, implying she can choose greatness.
memories.memory_text: I demanded hope from Dr Dee, and he told me that when the storm breaks, each person acts according to their nature—some flee, but some spread their wings like eagles and soar.

grounded_facts: After Dr Dee's metaphorical reassurance about human nature during crisis, Elizabeth regains confidence in her ability to face the coming struggle.
memories.memory_text: After hearing Dr Dee's words, I found my resolve again and knew I could face the coming struggle with strength.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth affirms Dr Dee's wisdom, and he reciprocates by honoring her stature, marking a moment of mutual respect.
memories.memory_text: I acknowledged Dr Dee's wisdom when I told him, 'You're a wise man, Dr Dee,' and he honored me in return by calling me a very great lady, which affirmed the mutual respect between us.

grounded_facts: A nighttime gathering of Queen Elizabeth and her key ministers to confront the threat of the Spanish Armada.
memories.memory_text: I stood at the window watching the beacon ignite, with Hatton, Howard, and Walsingham behind me, gathered in the night to face the coming threat.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth delivers a grave speech to her ministers, offering no comfort and emphasizing the existential threat of the Armada.
Elizabeth declares that England cannot be defeated by the Armada, expressing a solemn and resolute acceptance of national destiny and duty.
memories.memory_text: I told my ministers I could offer no words of comfort, for if the Armada succeeds, there will be no freedom left in our land and England will be no more — but I also declared that we cannot be defeated, accepting the duty that is ours.

grounded_facts: Queen Elizabeth commands that bells be rung in every church across the land.
memories.memory_text: I commanded that the bells be rung in every church across the land.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth gives Hatton the order to ring bells nationwide; he bows in acknowledgment.
memories.memory_text: I gave Hatton the order to ring bells nationwide, and I saw him bow in acknowledgment.

grounded_facts: Queen Elizabeth commands labourers to leave fields and take up arms, delaying the harvest.
memories.memory_text: I commanded the labourers to leave their fields and take up arms, knowing the harvest must wait.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth orders Hatton to mobilize labourers for arms, delaying the harvest; Hatton bows and leaves.
memories.memory_text: I ordered Hatton to mobilize the labourers for arms, and I watched him bow and leave to carry out my command.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth instructs Walsingham to release all prisoners, emphasizing national unity.
Queen Elizabeth commands the release of all prisoners, affirming their belonging to England.
memories.memory_text: I instructed Walsingham to release all prisoners, affirming that England is their country too, as an act of national unity.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth specifically orders Walsingham to release Raleigh and expresses her own desire for forgiveness.
Queen Elizabeth specifically orders the release of Raleigh and declares him forgiven, while expressing her own need for forgiveness.
memories.memory_text: I ordered Walsingham to release Raleigh and declared him forgiven, while also expressing my own need for forgiveness.

grounded_facts: A royal gathering in St Paul's Cathedral where Queen Elizabeth issues a series of national and personal commands during a moment of crisis.
memories.memory_text: I stood in St Paul's Cathedral and issued a series of commands during this moment of crisis, before continuing alone to the altar.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth orders her remaining entourage to leave so she can be alone at the altar.
memories.memory_text: I told my entourage to leave me, and I watched them bow and withdraw so I could be alone.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth dismisses her entourage and kneels alone before the altar, staring at God as an equal.
memories.memory_text: I went to the altar alone, knelt at the foot of the steps without bowing my head, and stared at God as I would an equal.

grounded_facts: Raleigh is handed a letter by a Royal Official and reads it, leading to his decision to join his ship.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Raleigh received a letter from a Royal Official and read it, which led to his decision to join his ship.

grounded_facts: Raleigh instructs the Royal Official to relay his intention to join his ship to the Queen.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Raleigh instructed the Royal Official to relay his intention to join his ship to me.

grounded_facts: After reading the letter, Raleigh decides to leave and join his ship.
memories.memory_text: I learned that after reading the letter, Raleigh decided to leave and join his ship.

grounded_facts: A gathering of the Queen and her advisers in her tent at Tilbury, where urgent naval reports are delivered.
memories.memory_text: I was in my tent at Tilbury with my advisers gathered around, waiting for urgent reports about the fleet.

grounded_facts: Queen Elizabeth demands to know whether the fleet has left Plymouth, showing urgency and concern about naval readiness.
Elizabeth demands information from her advisers about the fleet's status, expressing frustration at the lack of clear intelligence.
memories.memory_text: I demanded to know whether the fleet had left Plymouth, frustrated that such a simple question could not be answered clearly by my advisers.

grounded_facts: Admiral Winter delivers urgent news that the enemy has been engaged and two English ships have been lost.
memories.memory_text: I heard Admiral Winter report directly to me that the enemy had been engaged, majesty.

grounded_facts: The English fleet has engaged the enemy, resulting in a brave action but with the loss of two ships.
memories.memory_text: I was told of a brave action at sea, but we lost two of our ships in the engagement.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth publicly commits to sharing the fate of her soldiers, vowing to live or die with them in the upcoming battle.
memories.memory_text: I stood before my soldiers and declared that I would live or die among them in the battle, for England's fate is mine as much as theirs.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth addresses her soldiers with a powerful speech emphasizing unity, courage, and shared destiny.
A public address by Queen Elizabeth to her army on a hill above the camp, moments before engaging the enemy.
memories.memory_text: I stood before my soldiers on the hill and spoke to them of unity and courage, telling them I would live or die among them, that together we would face the enemy and not yield, and I declared myself their general, judge, and rewarder of virtues in the field.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth declares herself the general, judge, and rewarder of her soldiers' virtues in battle.
memories.memory_text: I declared that I myself would be the general, judge, and rewarder of every one of my soldiers' virtues in the field, standing with them in the battle to come.

grounded_facts: Raleigh asks Drake how many enemy ships are burning, seeking updated battlefield intelligence.
memories.memory_text: I asked Drake how many enemy ships were burning, trying to get a clear picture of our progress in the battle.

grounded_facts: Raleigh learns that four Spanish ships are burning and expresses that it is not enough, indicating his desire for greater victory.
memories.memory_text: I was told that four Spanish ships were burning, and I remember saying it wasn't enough—I wanted a greater victory.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth experiences the storm as a personal triumph, emotionally and spiritually connecting with it as a symbol of her victory.
memories.memory_text: I stood on the hill and let the storm wash over me, feeling it as my own triumph — the wind, the fury, it was all mine, and I embraced it as a sign of my victory.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth experiences a moment of triumph amidst the roaring wind above the English camp.
memories.memory_text: I felt a surge of triumph as I stood in the roaring wind above the English camp, knowing this moment was mine.

grounded_facts: A gathering of Walsingham's family and Elizabeth in his bedroom as he lies dying.
memories.memory_text: I saw Ursula and Mary standing in the background as I came to be with Walsingham, aware that his family was gathered around him.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth arrives at Walsingham's bedroom to see him in his final moments, expressing emotional concern.
memories.memory_text: I arrived at Walsingham's bedside, feeling deep concern as I looked down at him in his final moments.

grounded_facts: Walsingham is in his final moments, surrounded by family and Elizabeth, marking the recognition of his imminent death.
memories.memory_text: I could see that Walsingham was dying, his eyes closed and breaths shallow, surrounded by those who loved him.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth speaks to Walsingham with personal affection and sorrow, acknowledging their long-standing relationship.
memories.memory_text: I spoke to him with sorrow in my heart, calling him 'my old friend,' knowing how much our long bond meant in that moment.

grounded_facts: Walsingham, on his deathbed, asks Queen Elizabeth for permission to pass away, signaling his acceptance of death.
memories.memory_text: I was with Walsingham in his bedroom in London as he lay dying, and I heard him speak to me with difficulty before asking for my permission to pass away, signaling his acceptance of death.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth accepts Walsingham's impending death with emotional tenderness, recognizing his lifelong independence and service.
memories.memory_text: I told Walsingham I knew it, old friend, and not to leave me now, but then I acknowledged that he always did as he pleased, whether I wanted it or not, and I accepted that he would do as he pleased even in death, recognizing his lifelong independence and service.

grounded_facts: Walsingham asserts his autonomy even in dying, implying he no longer needs her command to leave.
memories.memory_text: Walsingham asked for my permission to go, yet in the same breath made it clear he no longer needed my command, asserting his autonomy even in dying, and I responded by affirming that he always did as he pleased, even from me.

grounded_facts: A private, emotionally charged encounter between Queen Elizabeth and her dying advisor Walsingham in his bedroom in London.
memories.memory_text: It was a private, emotionally charged encounter between me and my dying advisor Walsingham in his bedroom in London, where he spoke to me with difficulty, asked for permission to die, and I responded with tenderness, acknowledging his independence one last time.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth stoops down and kisses Walsingham's cheek as a final act of personal affection and farewell.
memories.memory_text: I stooped down and kissed Walsingham's cheek as a final act of personal affection and farewell.

grounded_facts: Queen Elizabeth makes a formal, unannounced visit to Raleigh's house, where she confronts the reality of his secret marriage and child.
memories.memory_text: I made a formal, unannounced visit to Raleigh's house and confronted the reality of his secret marriage and child.

grounded_facts: Raleigh's son was born four nights ago, marking a significant personal and political event given the illegitimate nature of the child and Bess's presence in his house.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Raleigh's son was born four nights ago, marking a significant personal and political event given the illegitimate nature of the child and Bess's presence in his house.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth silently forgives Bess for bearing Raleigh's child by touching her cheek, signaling the end of her displeasure.
memories.memory_text: I silently forgave Bess for bearing Raleigh's child by touching her cheek, signaling the end of my displeasure.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth inquires about the timing and health surrounding the birth, asserting her authority while gathering information.
memories.memory_text: I asked when the birth was, whether the mother was well, and about the child, asserting my authority while gathering information.

grounded_facts: Elizabeth probes whether Raleigh still holds onto his ambitions for the New World, testing his loyalty and emotional priorities.
memories.memory_text: I asked Raleigh if he still dreamed of his shining city in the New World, wanting to know where his heart truly lies.

grounded_facts: After initial coldness, Queen Elizabeth chooses to hold and bless Raleigh's newborn son, symbolically acknowledging the child and expressing emotional vulnerability.
memories.memory_text: I held Raleigh's newborn son in my arms and found myself more moved than I expected, blessing him as a gesture of grace.

grounded_facts: In voiceover, Elizabeth expresses her identity not as a mother but as a sovereign whose true treasure is her people's love.
memories.memory_text: I reflected that I may be called the Virgin Queen, but I have many children—my people—and there is no jewel I hold dearer than their love.

memories.memory_text: The Queen reached over and gently brushed a loose strand of hair from my face, her fingers warm against my cheek, and said, 'Don't hide your face.' I felt exposed, as if she could see right through me.

When the Queen asked what kind of man I wanted, I said I wanted an honest one, with friendly eyes and sweet breath—then I saw her smile, and I wondered if she suspected how much I already cared for someone.

I saw the Queen notice the lines around her mouth in the mirror, and when she asked when she ever smiled, I told her they were smile lines—then she smiled, and I couldn't help but smile back, seeing us both reflected there.

I watched Raleigh drop his cloak in the path of the Queen, pretending there was a puddle—no one else saw it, but I couldn’t help suppressing a smile, and when I glanced at him, I gave him a quick, secret smile as we passed.
I hurried into the Great Hall, curtsied, and said the puddle man was outside—just as I always did when he came, though I knew she’d chide me for being late again.
I said the Archduke was rather sweet, not thinking, and then felt my face warm when she turned and teased me, implying he was more suited to me than to her.

Raleigh bowed to us, but his eyes stayed on me—just me—and said he owed thanks to me for helping him, though I did nothing special. His voice was warm, and I felt my breath catch, unsure whether to look away or smile.
The Queen looked at me sharply and asked if I liked him, and my breath caught—I couldn’t deny it, not entirely, so I spoke of the New World instead.
I asked Raleigh if he was satisfied with the Queen's favor, and when he asked what I wanted, I met his eyes and told him I'd think of something—just before hurrying after Her Majesty.
I crept out of my bedroom, pulling the cloak tight around me, heart pounding with every step into the dark corridor.
I moved quietly through the dark corridor, stepping over the sleeping courtiers, heart pounding with every step, knowing if I were seen, it would mean ruin.

I moved through the dark alley, my cloak pulled tight, stepping over the sleeping bodies of the poor—afraid of being seen, afraid of what I was about to do. I checked the note in my hand, looked around once more, then knocked on the door and went inside.
I felt a chill when George pulled me into that embrace—his voice urgent, asking for my help to return to court, saying their lives depended on me.
I backed away, my voice trembling as I said, 'Don't put me in danger like this,' knowing I couldn't help him without risking everything.
I was walking with the other ladies, silent and anxious, when I saw Walsingham approaching—his glance cut through me, and when I dared to look back, he was still watching me, lingering in his gaze.
The Queen turned to me with a playful smile and asked if I wanted to go to sea, her eyes bright with amusement after teasing Mr. Raleigh.

I was holding the Queen’s hair out of the bathwater, gently stroking it without thinking—then I saw her watching me in the mirror, and I froze, unsure if I’d overstepped. She told me not to stop, her voice soft, almost tired, and I continued, my hands trembling slightly.

She asked me if anyone had ever truly liked her for herself—her voice quiet, searching—and then said she envied me, that I was free to have what she could not. I didn’t speak, only kept stroking her hair, feeling the weight of her words settle in my chest.
When Walsingham said the traitor had talked, I felt a jolt inside—my cousin’s name hung in the air unspoken, but I knew. My hands went cold, and I couldn’t look up.
I told Raleigh he was sulking like a child, and I meant it—his turning away from the Queen in her danger felt like a betrayal, not just of her but of everything I’ve sacrificed to stay loyal.
I told him to go to the Queen as her friend—those words came from somewhere deep, a plea not just for her safety but for him to remember who he once was to her.

I was on my knees at the chapel altar, praying in silence, when I felt his presence—Raleigh had come in. I turned and told him my prayer was done, but I couldn’t look him in the eyes when I admitted I gave information about my cousin because I was afraid.

After he wiped away my tear, I couldn’t hold back anymore—I threw myself into his arms, sobbing. When I kissed his hand and then our lips met, it wasn’t just comfort we were seeking, but something deeper, long denied.
I was with Raleigh at his house as it grew dark.

I jumped into the air during La Volta, spinning with my feet flying out, and when the dancing master lowered me down, I could feel everyone’s eyes on me—I loved the thrill of it, the way the court laughed and clapped.

Raleigh held me by the waist, his hands firm as I jumped, and when he swung me round during the dance, I felt the closeness between us—the rhythm, the warmth—knowing the Queen was watching but unable to ignore the spark.

I told the Queen that Mary would keep lying until her traitor's heart was cut out, and when Elizabeth looked at me in surprise, I said I used to be quieter—because the truth needed to be spoken, no matter how harsh.
I felt Raleigh's hand close around mine as I told him the Queen was suffering, and I urged him to go to her, though she had refused everyone.

I felt the weight of her body as she collapsed, and my arms went around her instinctively—Raleigh’s hands were there too, holding her up, and for that breath we were one in the grief I could not name.
I touched my waist and told him I'm pregnant—no one knows, and I’ve made my plans to leave court quietly, to go to my mother’s house and live in hiding.
I told him to forget me, to go to his ship and do his duty—my voice was steady, but my heart broke saying it, knowing we could never be.

I remember the cold touch of the ring as Walter slid it slowly from my thumb to my ring finger, each movement a whispered vow beneath the priest’s blessing—my breath trembling, my heart certain and afraid.

memories.memory_text: I remember the weight of their eyes as they pressed me to spill my cousin’s blood—how Howard’s voice tightened on 'while she lives,' as if her mere breath were treason. I felt the crown heavy on my head, and I asked them, 'What is her crime?'
I stood before my council and said plainly that I would not punish people for their beliefs, only for their deeds, and that I meant to earn the love of my people, not rule through fear.
I turned to Bess and asked what kind of man she wanted, then added that she’d want good legs—something light, almost teasing, to deflect Walsingham’s insistence that I produce an heir.
I leaned over and brushed a stray lock of hair from Bess’s face. I told her, 'Don’t hide your face.'

I walked into St Paul's with Walsingham at my side, the nave vast and hollow around us, and told him plainly—I know the dangers better than any councillor. The shipbuilders in Spanish ports, the crumbling wall at Dover—no coin to mend it. I don’t need them to teach me my own realm’s peril.

At the foot of the altar, I knelt and reached my hand back without looking—I knew Bess would be there. When she took it, I said, 'Let’s pray, Bess,' and we did, together, for wisdom not to fear shadows, and courage when true danger comes. I felt her presence, steady, as I spoke.
I reached out to bless a child thrust forward by its mother, my fingers brushing the infant’s head as the crowd roared—some with love, some with hate, their cries tangled in my ears.

Raleigh laid his cloak on the ground before me, claiming a puddle, but I saw none—only his boldness—so I stepped over it without a word, meeting his eyes just long enough to let him feel the weight of my silence.
I said 'Send for him' after considering the portrait of Archduke Charles, and then asked Bess to find out where he was—my voice was calm, but I felt a flicker of something like anticipation.

When Don Guerau accused Raleigh of piracy, I watched him kneel and then rise at my gesture, his hampers full of Spanish goods—I said 'Ah, yes. Raleigh. I've heard of your voyage,' though I hadn't yet heard the details.

I noticed the Archduke barely touched his food, so I shared my trick—pretending there's a pane of glass between us and the court, speaking to him in German to ease his shyness, and testing whether he could meet me in that quiet honesty.
I saw Bess staring at Raleigh as he flirted with the ladies, and when I followed her gaze, I felt a spark of intrigue—so I told her quietly, 'He interests me. Talk to him.'

I sat still, listening to Raleigh’s voice as he spoke of crossing the ocean—his words pulled my gaze outward, as if I could see that endless horizon myself, vast and empty, with only a speck of a ship beneath it.
I told them to wait—let the Archduke and all the court stand—because I needed to hear Raleigh’s voice, to follow that fragile hope he spoke of, rising like a haze on the western sea.
I danced with Raleigh while his voice spoke of distant shores. After the music ended, I sat and listened as he described the New World.
He spoke of land rising from the horizon like resurrection, and I sat very still — the word 'New World' echoed in me, not as conquest, but as a second birth, something long dead waking.
I stood before my court and spoke the words that would carry the weight of a nation's future—'The Queen lives for her people'—and in that moment, I offered my solitude as a crown.
I told him I liked him, standing there beneath the vast murals, and for a moment I let myself be seen not as a queen, but as a woman who might be drawn to another.
When he said I might not know the pleasure of being liked for myself, I felt exposed—so I cut him off, saying he had become dull, though it was my own fear I sought to silence.
I caught Raleigh off guard when I told him he was lying—'You don't want me on your ship at all'—and saw the surprise flash in his eyes.
After that charged look with Raleigh, I turned to Bess and said we must persuade him to stay—feeling the relief of shifting from dangerous intimacy to safer alliance.

I felt the warmth of the bath and the soft pull of Bess’s hands on my hair, and in the mirror, I saw her stroking my tresses—unaware at first that I was watching. I asked her if anyone has ever truly liked me for myself, not for my crown or power.

Looking at Bess in the mirror, I told her I envied her—her freedom to have what I cannot. I said it’s all over so soon, as if youth and life pass quickly, and I felt the weight of what I’ve had to give up.

I named the 'Enterprise of England' before the Spanish Ambassador, calling it by its true name—'la Empresa di Inglaterra'—and declared it a Spanish plot, Philip’s own design to invade and overthrow me.
I turned on Raleigh in fury, demanding he lower his eyes—I am the Queen—and swept past him, my rage still trembling in my limbs.
I rose to face the pistol, and he hesitated—his hand trembled, his eyes locked on mine, and when the shot rang out, I felt no pain. I stood unharmed, and he broke before me.
I remember thinking about Mary’s chestnut hair and hazel eyes, wondering if she truly was taller than me—people lie when they say I’m beautiful, so why wouldn’t they lie about her?
When Bess said Mary would lie until her traitor's heart was cut out, I looked at her in shock—she used to be gentler, and I couldn’t hide my surprise at how hardened she had become.
I sat there with my eyes closed, feeling the weight of what I must do—signing a queen’s death warrant—and whispered that I owe England my life, but they must not ask for my soul.
I demanded Dr Dee tell me again his prophecy — I would not let England fall while I am Queen, and I shouted that I would not be a toy of the fates, not after surviving an assassin's bullet.

After my anger passed, I asked him only whether any outcome was possible — I needed hope, and when he spoke of men rising like eagles in the storm, I felt myself stand taller, certain again of who I am.
I watched the last beacon catch fire outside the window. My ministers stood behind me. I turned to them and spoke of the danger we faced.

I turned to my lords and spoke what had to be said—no comfort, only truth: if the Armada prevails, England ends. And in that moment, I could not afford to be afraid; I was no longer a woman trembling at firelight, but the resolve of a nation.
I touched Bess's cheek—just lightly—and said nothing. There was no need for words; she understood.
I took the baby into my arms, held him carefully, and pressed my cheek to his head. I closed my eyes, moved in that moment, and thought: you are all my children.

memories.memory_text: I stood at the prow of the Tyger, wind in my face, and gave the order—'Let England know we're back.' Then the roar of the broadside tore across the water, echoing off the white cliffs.
She spoke to me—just two words, but they were meant for me. I could feel the weight of it, a crack in the armor of court, and Calley knew it too.
There was a girl behind her—pale, still, watching. I don’t know her name, but the sight of her pulled me like a current after years at sea.
I was stopped at the door, demanding to see the Lord Chamberlain, but the doorkeeper just stood there, telling me I had to wait with the rest of the petitioners—no way to know when he'd come out.
Just as I was about to lose patience, Bess Throckmorton ran past, saw me, and gave me a quick smile—light, knowing—before disappearing inside.

I presented the Queen with mud and leaves—potatoes and tobacco—simple things to her, but symbols of a new world I’d fought to reach. Her amusement masked the weight of what they truly were: the promise of life and land beyond the sea.

Only after the mud and leaves did I reveal the gold—real Spanish gold—pulling a coin from the final basket. I said nothing of piracy; the gleam in the Queen’s eye told me she already understood: this was not theft, but service rendered in her name.

I saw her there among the ladies—Bess—laughing about 'patata' and mud, then going quiet when they noticed me. When she said, 'Well, wouldn't you?', I knew she was looking at me differently, and I had to speak to her.
After I thanked her, all the ladies curtseyed—proper, formal—but I noticed how they glanced back at me as they walked away, like I was someone new, someone seen.
I stood before the Queen, though she did not speak to me directly—her questions about my motives were for Bess, not me, and I could only wait, knowing my fate turned on words not yet spoken.
I walked into the antechamber and saw the door keeper bow, then open the doors for me—no hesitation, no delay—just passage granted, as if I belonged there.
I asked her if she could imagine crossing an ocean, and I spoke of the horizon stretching empty in every direction, our ship no more than a speck in the vastness.
I remember speaking to her about hope—how it feels when everything screams that you're lost, and still you stare west, hoping against reason, the sun in your eyes day after day.
Elizabeth told Hatton to let them wait and told me to go on speaking.

I danced with her, the Queen, moving through the dim light of her private quarters—her hand in mine, the music guiding us, and all the while I could feel her listening, not just to the steps but to something deeper I was about to say.

After the music stopped, I told her—'Land. Life. Resurrection.'—and I saw it in her eyes: the weight of her crown, the silence of her solitude, and how those words reached something she couldn't name.
I told her I liked her, straight and plain, after she said she liked me—I saw the surprise in her eyes, how unaccustomed she was to such honesty.
When she offered to reward me, I asked her to reward the mission instead—then said being free to like her was my true reward, and I saw her flinch, as if I'd come too close to something private.

Walsingham stepped in beside me in the hallway, warning me not to ask for too much—like I was just another greedy courtier. I told him he thinks I'm a cynical adventurer with no breeding, but I'm not wrong about what I am—I said it straight, and he almost smiled.
I stood waiting for her, and when she entered, there was a flush on her cheeks—she said she had been waiting too. Then Walsingham came, and duty took her from me.
I was writing my letter to the Queen at the chart table, the pen moving fast—putting down my request to return to the New World, knowing it meant stepping away from court for good.
Bess stood before me, fierce and unflinching, calling me out for sulking like a child when the Queen needed me—her voice cut through my pride, and I felt the weight of my own pettiness.
I knelt as she said 'Kneel,' and felt the light tap of her hand on my shoulder—then rose as Sir Walter Raleigh, a title I hadn't sought and didn't expect to carry in this gilded cage.
She asked why I couldn't look at her, then admitted she was vain and needed admiration. She said she would follow me to the New World if she could.
I was with Bess in my house at dusk, and we made love.
I met the Queen’s gaze and said she eats and drinks control — and when she challenged me with 'Do you say so?', I held my ground, though the air tightened around us.
I lifted Bess into the spin, her body close, her feet flying as we turned — I could feel the Queen’s eyes on us, measuring every movement, allowing it only because she commanded it.
I looked at her as she sat turned away, and asked, 'Since when were you so afraid?'—then held my silence as she finally turned to face me.

I told her, 'We mortals have many weaknesses. We feel too much. Hurt too much. And all too soon, we die. But we do have the chance of love,' and saw her close her eyes as if carrying the weight of it.
I saw her come rushing out, tears in her eyes, and then she looked at me and said, 'I want it stopped!'—as if I could do something, as if I were the one who could change it all.
I held her tightly as she thrashed and shouted, her voice breaking—'No! It must be stopped!'—and I felt the weight of her fear in my arms.
I saw her hand touch her waist, and the word caught in my throat—'pregnant?'—as if saying it might make it real, and suddenly the world narrowed to that quiet corner in the chaos of the palace.
She asked me to forget her—to go to my ship, do my duty, and let her go—and I could only whisper 'Oh, Bess...' as the weight of what she was giving up, what I was losing, pressed down on me.

I slid the ring from her thumb to her forefinger, then to her index, each time speaking the words that bound us—father, son, spirit—until it settled on her ring finger, and I said 'Amen,' my voice steady despite the weight of what we'd done.

I lay there in my prison clothes, waiting, when the servant came in with food and said the Spanish were off Portland—then that the fleet was at Plymouth, with Drake and all the rest. I could only say, 'All but me,' and feel the weight of being left behind.
